name: Ahira
title: Chieftain and tribal prince of the tribe of Naphtali
summary: Ahira, son of Enan, was appointed by God as tribal prince (נָשִׂיא, nasi) over Naphtali during Israel's wilderness journey. He assisted Moses in the census and in organizing the camp and march. As commander of Naphtali's military division, he also bore military responsibility, and his tribe took the last position in the marching order – behind Dan's banner on the north side of the tabernacle. When the altar of the tabernacle was dedicated, Ahira brought forward his offering on the twelfth and final day. The fact that his gifts were identical to those of the other tribal leaders emphasizes that every tribe stood equally before God in their worship. Although Ahira is mentioned only in a few passages in Numbers, the description portrays him as a leader who faithfully carried out the task entrusted to him.

keyEvents.title: Appointed as Leader of Naphtali
keyEvents.description: God appointed Ahira, son of Enan, as leader of the tribe of Naphtali to assist Moses with the census of Israel.

keyEvents.title: Census of the Tribe of Naphtali
keyEvents.description: Under Ahira's leadership, the tribe of Naphtali was counted, and the number of men able to serve in the army from twenty years old and upward was 53,400.

keyEvents.title: Naphtali's Camp Position and Marching Order
keyEvents.description: Ahira led the tribe of Naphtali in their assigned position on the north side of the tabernacle under the banner of Dan, both within the camp and as the last division in the marching order when breaking camp.

keyEvents.title: Ahira's Offering at the Dedication of the Altar
keyEvents.description: On the twelfth and final day of the altar dedication, Ahira brought his offering, consisting of a silver plate, a silver basin, a gold bowl with incense, a burnt offering, a sin offering, and a peace offering—identical to the gifts of the other tribal leaders.

keyEvents.title: Commander of Naphtali's Military Division
keyEvents.description: Ahira, son of Enan, led the military division of the tribe of Naphtali when Israel's camp broke up from the wilderness of Sinai.

versions.summary: Ahira, son of Enan, was the chosen leader (chief) of the tribe of Naphtali during Israel's journey through the wilderness. He was appointed by God to assist Moses with the census and with organizing Israel's camp. He also brought his offering at the dedication of the tabernacle's altar.

versions.summary: Ahira, son of Enan, was appointed by God as leader (נָשִׂיא, nasi) over the tribe of Naphtali during Israel's time in the wilderness. His task was to assist Moses with the census and with organizing Israel's camp and march. As commander of Naphtali's military division, he also bore military responsibility, and his tribe received the last position in the marching order, under Dan's banner on the north side of the tabernacle. At the dedication of the tabernacle altar, Ahira brought his offering on the twelfth and final day, identical to the gifts from the other tribal leaders—a clear expression that all tribes stood equal in their worship of God. Although Ahira is mentioned briefly in the biblical account, his faithful execution of his duties testifies to a leader who fulfilled his God-given role with loyalty.

footnotes.text: The name Ahira (אֲחִירַע) is composed of אָח ('akh', brother) and an element that can be linked to either רֵעַ ('rea', friend/neighbor) or רַע ('ra', evil). Most scholars prefer the interpretation 'my brother is a friend' based on parallel Semitic naming patterns where the second element is often positive. The uncertainty arises because the consonantal text allows for both readings.

The title נָשִׂיא (nasi) used for Ahira and the other tribal leaders in Numbers denotes an exalted leader or prince. The word is derived from the root נשא ('to lift up, exalt'). In the biblical context, the title refers to tribal chiefs with political, military, and religious authority. In rabbinic tradition, the title was later used for the head of the Sanhedrin.

The fact that Ahira brought his offering on the twelfth and final day of the altar dedication (Num 7:78–83) reflects Naphtali's position as the last tribe in the camp arrangement. The order of the offerings followed the established camp layout from Num 2, demonstrating the systematic organization of Israel's tribal camp in the wilderness.

Each tribal leader brought identical offerings at the altar dedication—emphasizing the equality among the tribes in their worship of God, despite differences in tribe size and position. Theologically, this signals that no tribe held precedence before God.

The tribe of Naphtali was part of the northern camp division under Dan's banner (Num 2:25–31). This military organization with four camp divisions around the tabernacle has parallels to Egyptian and Mesopotamian military camp structures from the second millennium BCE, a point discussed in archaeological and historical research.

Enan (אֵינָן), Ahira's father, bears a name likely derived from the root עין ('ayin', eye/spring), possibly meaning 'he has eyes' or 'spring'. The name appears exclusively as a patronym for Ahira in the biblical texts.
